source.title: Harmonic Loss Trains Interpretable AI Models
source.authors: David D. Baek; Zi-Ming Liu; Riya Tyagi; Max Tegmark

record.tranche_reason: The study measures delayed generalization on algorithmic tasks using epochs to train- and test-accuracy thresholds, and compares how it changes with harmonic versus standard loss. This is a conceptual test of grokking, not a reproduction of the original training recipe.
record.gate_note: The relevant results are the grokking comparisons in Figures 3(c), 4, and 14. The data-fraction plots measure test accuracy versus training-set fraction, not how grokking delay changes with training-set size, so they are not rows for V1. Other loss, interpretability, and GPT-2 results do not measure the behaviors named by the claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study measures delayed generalization (epochs to test acc >0.9 vs to train acc >0.9) on small algorithmic tasks for standard cross-entropy MLPs and transformers. It reports severe grokking in standard MLPs and shows that harmonic loss largely removes it. It also shows that a standard MLP needs weight decay to generalize at all. This is a different method aimed at the same question, not the original recipe.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude harmonic loss reduces grokking overall, most evidently on modular addition and permutation composition, where standard MLPs grok severely. In the modular-addition case study, the harmonic MLP generalizes quickly without grokking or weight decay, while the standard MLP needs strong weight decay and then groks. They attribute this to harmonic loss's finite convergence point (non-diverging weight norm).
record.recipe_differences: The study compares standard cross-entropy training with a new harmonic-loss training procedure. It measures epochs to cross accuracy thresholds rather than reproducing the original study's full training recipe; it also compares loss types and includes multiple synthetic tasks and architectures.
record.method_sensitivity: Loss type changes the reported grokking behavior. The modular-addition case study also varies weight decay: the standard MLP often fails to generalize at weight decay=0, while weight decay=0.5 permits generalization but has significant grokking.

fits_no_version.finding: Harmonic models reach higher test accuracy at smaller training fractions than standard models (Fig. 3b, 14b); the measure is final accuracy, not delay.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Loss geometry (distance-based logits, scale-invariant normalization) changes the data needed to generalize on algorithmic tasks.

record.problems: The grokking comparisons are presented in plots without numeric values or uncertainty intervals. Runs that did not achieve 90% accuracy were omitted from the threshold comparison. The study does not test how grokking delay varies with training-set size.

untested.parts: Whether the delay grows as the training set shrinks. Full chance-to-near-perfect trajectories are shown only in a Figure 4 illustration.

missing.what: Grokking comparison for standard vs harmonic transformers, and for the other tasks (in-context learning, equivalence classes, genealogy), epochs-to-threshold scatter
missing.locator: Appendix F, Figure 14(c); Section 3.4 'harmonic loss overall reduces grokking'

record.verdict_notes: All grokking evidence is figure-only with no numbers or uncertainty, and runs below 90% are omitted, which could hide non-generalizing runs. R7 could also be read as consistent with V5's 'another bias toward low norm': the authors attribute harmonic loss's effect to a plateauing weight norm. I did not label this because it is interpretive. Not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test whether the delay grows as the training set shrinks, or report full accuracy trajectories demonstrating a chance-to-near-perfect jump after training accuracy saturates.
